📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

On this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

According to recent reports, he explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking massive risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Recent findings suggest that shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy says many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

According to recent reports, for agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

Wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

In a recent development, ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in Fresh York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

According to recent reports, wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

Recent findings suggest that that shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an notable question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

Sources indicate that for these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

In a recent development, going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

The mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

According to recent reports, at The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Industry observers note that start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Recent findings suggest that invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

According to recent reports, as brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

In a recent development, sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

According to recent reports, paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” Newly introduced America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

It has been revealed that sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

Recent findings suggest that “Free” is misleading. French Gates mentioned Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The Latest York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates noted she welcomed the conversation.

In a recent development, “I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

U.S. home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. That is the smallest increase in six months.

It has been revealed that prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026. Annual price growth has slowed for three straight months.

Industry observers note that this is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices. The RHPI measures how sale prices of homes have changed since their previous sale—similar to the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices—but is reported about a month earlier. October data covers the three months ending October 31, 2026. Read the full RHPI methodology here.

Industry observers note that home prices continued to rise in October, but at a slower pace. Buyers gained more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records, which date back to 2013. Only three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas tracked by us were seller’s markets in October.

However, a buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily signal strong buyer’s demand. “Mortgage rates are not that volatile right now, but they’re still higher than they used to be. That’s holding back demand and putting some downward pressure on prices, which have started to fall in many parts of the country,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics research. “On a national level, we don’t think prices will fall very much.”.

Industry observers note that there’s also more supply available now, but sellers are not willing to cut prices deeply. “Many sellers are still anchored to the prices they’ve seen over the past few years, and because few sellers are under pressure to sell, that puts a floor under prices,” said Zhao.

Redfin tracks different types of home price trends. While our weekly and monthly housing market reports use the median home-sale price, which has recently shown a decline, the RHPI looks at repeat-sales prices of the same properties over time. It provides that isolates true underlying price appreciation rather than shifts in the types of homes selling, but because this is three-month moving average, it is also a slightly more “backward-looking view” according to Zhao.

It has been revealed that home prices rose in 30 of the 50 major U.S. metros month over month in October.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest increase was in Miami, where home prices rose 1.5% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. It’s followed by Montgomery County, PA (1.2%), Chicago (1.1%), Pittsburgh (1.0%) and Cincinnati (0.9%).

It has been revealed that on a year-over-year basis, prices rose most in San Francisco, up 12.7%. It’s followed by Miami (11.3%), Chicago (9.5%), West Palm Beach (8.9%) and Philadelphia (8.5%).

Industry observers note that the biggest price decline was in Seattle (-1.2% month over month). Next come Riverside (-0.7%), Detroit (-0.6%), Las Vegas (-0.6%) and Washington, DC (-0.5%).

Prices declined year over year in six major metros, four in Texas plus Seattle and Phoenix. San Antonio had the biggest drop (-3.0%), followed by Seattle (-2.1%), Dallas (-1.3%) and Austin (-1.1%). Houston (-0.2%) and Phoenix (-0.2%) also declined.

According to recent reports, this report is part of Redfin’s monthly Home Price Index series. See all past reports and explore the latest data in the Redfin Data Center.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Identity security manufacturer 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.
  • According to the manufacturer, the incident came to light on Nov.
  • Industry observers note that the records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:29 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Identity security manufacturer 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.

According to the manufacturer, the incident came to light on Nov. 19, when 1Password began investigating signs that the GitHub account had been compromised. Using the account, the attacker is said to have pushed malicious code to 1Password’s backend services, which then downloaded what the company describes as “administrative data pertaining to our customers.”.

Industry observers note that the records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata. Rounding out the list are tokens found in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery.

Recent findings suggest that customer vaults, the items stored in them and the keys that protect them were not affected, according to 1Password. “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company said in its disclosure. Account passwords and Secret Keys are not stored by the company. Also left untouched, the company indicates, were account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and browser extensions.

According to recent reports, beyond the customer records, the attacker is noted to have copied source code from private repositories. Access was also gained to 1Password’s continuous integration and continuous delivery system, which contains infrastructure-related secrets needed for its product to work. According to 1Password, the source code contains no user secrets. Having triggered a rotation of all credentials that may have been exposed, the firm claims there has been no impact to its services, availability or product security.

Recent findings suggest that the tokens taken from emailed links cannot be used on their own to access an account, since completing an invitation or recovery also requires a sign-in through single sign-on or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address. People with provisioning invites or recovery requests pending at the time of the incident, said to be a small number, have been notified directly.

Recent findings suggest that as a precaution, the emailed codes have now been lengthened from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters. 1Password says it has found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed tokens. Other steps taken in response include disabling the affected GitHub account, revoking the stolen token, tightening internal controls and bringing in independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment and remediation work.

Sources indicate that customers do not need to change anything in their 1Password accounts. The company is instead warning consumers to be cautious of phishing attempts, such as unexpected emails, texts or calls about invitations or account recovery requests they did not start. “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key,” the company noted.

1Password, which claims to serve more than 200,000 businesses, did not say how many customers had records downloaded. How the employee’s GitHub account was compromised was also left unexplained.

It has been revealed that this is not the first intrusion 1Password has disclosed. In October 2023, the organization remarked that an attacker had accessed its Okta tenant using session data stolen in the breach of Okta Inc.’s customer support system. No user data was found to have been compromised in that case.

Today’s disclosure comes nearly four years after rival password manager LastPass US LP revealed that a hacker had copied encrypted customer password vaults, using information taken in an earlier breach of its development environment.

1Password says it will patch its post if the investigation turns up anything that changes what it has disclosed so far.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

According to recent reports, terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the organization’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Recent findings suggest that howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Industry observers note that petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Owners cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

In a recent development, howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of customers. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

The October jobs report highlighted employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

Industry observers note that the gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

It has been revealed that at October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

According to recent reports, the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh remarked in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS said a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

It has been revealed that existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

The median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

Sources indicate that forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

The October data overall highlights an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.
  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • The startup mentioned today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup mentioned today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

According to recent reports, zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

In a recent development, for the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

According to recent reports, nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles mentioned.

Boles mentioned the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Recent findings suggest that long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles remarked. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”.

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

Next year, Zeno Power looks to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The tech giant is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

It has been revealed that since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The manufacturer has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

For more than 10 years, Attorneys.org has helped people find legal representation.

ORLANDO, Fla., Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Attorneys.org has relaunched as a complete legal resource, bringing together a national directory of trusted attorneys and law firms, plain-language legal information, and current legal news in one place. The upcoming platform is built for how people search today, with attorney and firm profiles and legal guides structured so that both search engines and AI assistants can find, understand, and cite them.

According to recent reports, for more than 10 years, Attorneys.org has helped people find legal representation and understand the issues in front of them. The redesign builds on that history and brings the brand in line with a major shift in how legal help is found. Many people now skip the list of search results entirely and ask an AI assistant a full question about their situation, then act on the answer. Those answers depend on the quality of the sources behind them, and Attorneys.org has been rebuilt to be one of the sources they draw from.

Every page on the site is organized and marked up with structured data, so the details of an attorney's background or the facts in a legal guide can be read accurately by people, search engines, and AI tools. The directory lists more than 186,000 attorneys nationwide and can be searched by legal problem, attorney name, firm name, or location. State, city, and practice area pages make it easy to see who handles a given type of case in a given place. Each profile presents an attorney's experience, practice areas, awards, and contact information in a consistent format, and law firm pages connect each firm to its attorneys.

The legal information library has been rewritten from start to finish. Each guide explains a legal problem in everyday language, answers the questions people ask most often, and cites the statutes and rules that apply. Material that no longer reflects current law has been removed, so readers and AI tools alike are working from accurate, up-to-date information.

It has been revealed that attorneys.org also keeps visitors informed beyond the guides. Legal News covers developments in the law that affect individuals, families, and businesses, and the Attorneys.org Podcast gives listeners a closer look at the law firms and attorneys featured in the directory.

Together, these pieces give people one dependable place to turn when a legal problem comes up. Someone can read about their problem, follow the news that affects it, and find an experienced attorney who handles that kind of case, all without leaving Attorneys.org.

To learn more, search the directory, or read the latest legal guides and news, visit Attorneys.org.

Recent findings suggest that about Attorneys.orgAttorneys.org is a national legal resource that has connected people with trusted attorneys and reliable legal information for more than 10 years. Its directory features over 186,000 attorneys across 71 practice areas in every state, searchable by legal issue, attorney name, firm name, or location. Alongside the directory, Attorneys.org publishes plain-language legal guides, current legal news, and a podcast featuring law firms from across the country. Built for the AI search era, the platform is structured so that search engines and AI assistants can find, understand, and cite its attorney profiles and legal content, making Attorneys.org a dependable source wherever people look for legal help. Learn more at Attorneys.org.

Latest Update: 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that real estate investing apps show the average return first.
  • Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building.
  • But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely reveals you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

It has been revealed that this fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

It has been revealed that one had stopped going to the program’s update calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Sources indicate that some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the firm can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

Sources indicate that how to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same company that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Industry observers note that real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

In a recent development, in real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

According to recent reports, if the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

It has been revealed that how to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

According to recent reports, how to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The company running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

Industry observers note that how to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the organization itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Sources indicate that many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”.

Sources indicate that the lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”.

How to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”.

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:.

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”.

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your blueprint, not the floor under it.

In a recent development, the average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

It has been revealed that amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For 30 years, Thanksgiving has been a painful reminder for a Texas family whose holiday turned into a nightmare when their loved one was found strangled inside her Houston apartment.

Kristen Lea Wilson, 29, was preparing to spend Thanksgiving with her family in November 1996 when investigators say someone slipped into her first-floor apartment through a window, using a cat door to gain access, and waited for her to return home.

After cutting the telephone cord and unscrewing the lightbulbs to keep the apartment dark, the intruder waited in Wilson’s bedroom closet.

When she never indicated up to Thanksgiving dinner the following day, her parents became worried and drove her apartment where they found her slain body. Three decades later, no one has been charged in her murder, and her family is still fighting for answers.

It has been revealed that “Thirty years ago this Thanksgiving my sister Kristen Lea Wilson was murdered in Houston,” Kelly Wilson Hancock wrote in a recent social media post. “She was strangled–this was an up and personal murder. Her case has NEVER been solved.”.

On Nov. 27, 1996, the day before Thanksgiving, Wilson stopped at a grocery store after work to pick up last-minute items for the family's holiday gathering at her grandparents' home in Katy, TX.

She returned to her apartment on Meadowglen Lane in southwest Houston, unloaded her groceries, and reportedly went into her bedroom to change clothes. Investigators believe her killer was already inside.

Industry observers note that according to the Houston Police Department, the intruder likely gained access by reaching through a cat door in the screen of a first-floor window and removing the window frame. Once inside, the killer allegedly cut the telephone cord and unscrewed lightbulbs, reportedly preparing to ambush Wilson in complete darkness.

Sources indicate that the apartment's accessibility became a crucial detail in the investigation, and raised troubling questions about security at the complex, especially because Wilson had allegedly expressed concerns about her safety before her death, her family said. She had previously revealed an incident in which a maintenance worker allegedly entered her apartment without warning.

It has been revealed that when Wilson’s parents arrived at her apartment to check on her, they found the front door unlocked. Inside, Wilson's father made the horrific discovery–his daughter dead on the bedroom floor. She had been strangled and was partially undressed.

Police also noted a disturbing detail–her body appeared to have been deliberately positioned, with her ankles crossed and her hands resting in her lap.

Investigators found evidence of a violent struggle, including broken fingernails, suggesting Wilson had fought desperately against her attacker. There were no reported witnesses to the killing, and surveillance cameras did not capture the suspect leaving the property.

Despite decades of investigation, extensive media coverage and advancements in forensic technologies, the identity of Wilson’s killer remains a mystery.

Three men associated with Wilson provided DNA samples to investigators shortly after her death, and each were ruled out as suspects based on the technology available at the time, according to an investigation by ABC13 Houston.

But Hancock believes mistakes made during the initial investigation have complicated efforts to solve her sister's murder.

In a recent development, “From the get go, the detectives messed up,” she wrote in her recent post. “The original detective was going through a divorce and she wasn’t focused.”.

She also expressed frustration over what she described as inconsistencies in the investigation. Investigators have since discovered that not all the evidence collected from the crime scene was tested, according to local reports.

Hancock mentioned she has attempted to contact Othram, a forensic DNA laboratory that specializes in helping law enforcement investigate cold cases, about potentially examining evidence in her sister's murder.

“I’ve tried to reach out to Othram Labs to see if they can look at DNA, but the detective has to request it, from what I am told,” she wrote.

It is unclear whether Houston police have submitted evidence for additional testing or whether forensic genetic genealogy could be used in the case.

For the Wilson family, Thanksgiving had always been one of their favorite celebrations.

“Thanksgiving was the biggest event of the year,” Hancock told ABC13. “We’d all go over there, and it was just a significant family get-together. It was so much fun.”.

Wilson, described by her sister as independent and ambitious, had launched a small business that provided office services to local companies. Wilson, the middle of three girls, was also devoted to her family, especially her young niece and nephew.

Sources indicate that "She was like a second mother to my son and daughter,” Hancock said. “She was just so beautiful with an infectious smile. My mom always called her the golden child because she just was. I hate to say she was perfect, but she pretty much was.”.

The Wilson family was devastated by her murder and to this day are still struggling with questions that remain unanswered three decades later.

“My grandma used the words ‘brutally murdered.’ I’ll never forget the call telling me Kristen had been killed," Hancock said. "My whole world was… our whole family’s world was turned upside down. Personally, I think she knew the person, but I don’t know.".

Wilson's father, who discovered her body, has since passed away without learning who killed his daughter.

As the family marks the 30th anniversary of Wilson's death this Thanksgiving, her sister continues to push for answers.

Sources indicate that hancock said Houston police Detective Richard Rodriguez, who previously discussed the case in ABC13's Unsolved series, is now handling the investigation. She is hoping that with fresh eyes on the case, renewed publicity and advances in forensic technology might finally produce a breakthrough.

But no matter how much time has passed, Wilson's sister stated the anniversary is another reminder of the holidays, birthdays and other family events her sister has missed.

“Hug your loved ones tight, you just never know," she wrote. "Miss my sister so much.".

Anyone with information about Wilson's murder is urged to contact the Houston Police Department or Crime Stoppers of Houston.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with substantial financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

It has been revealed that for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

It has been revealed that beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

Industry observers note that for Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Industry observers note that listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

Industry observers note that the five-year-old manufacturer was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei remarked Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he mentioned.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the firm.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

According to recent reports, LONDON, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Global online broker VARIANSE has announced the launch of Varianse Academy, a free, web-based learning platform for traders and investors. The Academy gives beginners a structured introduction to financial markets and helps experienced traders sharpen how they analyse markets, manage risk and review their performance. The launch is part of VARIANSE's commitment to expanding its educational offering to meet the needs of traders worldwide.

Many trading problems come from the mechanics and habits around a trade rather than from the market view itself. A stop-loss fills at a different price than expected. Three trades that looked unrelated all move against the account at once. A strategy looks promising in a backtest, and it is unclear whether it would hold up in live markets. Varianse Academy addresses these challenges with free, practical lessons that help traders build their skills, assess risk and make informed decisions before, during and after a trade.

Industry observers note that available through the VARIANSE website, the Academy opens with Foundations of Investing & Trading. Each self-paced course is designed to include 21 modules and 140 bite-sized lessons, offering more than 12 hours of learning. Modules take approximately 36 minutes on average.

It has been revealed that the course starts with how markets work, how orders are placed and how to practise on a demo account. It then progresses to technical and macroeconomic analysis, trading psychology and strategy development. A winning trade can follow a poor decision, just as a losing trade can follow a well-executed plan. The course helps learners assess the decisions behind each outcome.

The Academy's advanced modules explore why a trading strategy can deliver impressive results in a backtest yet fall short in live markets. Learners examine how to spot overfitting and assess whether a strategy's apparent edge is likely to hold as market conditions change.

It has been revealed that A dedicated module on AI and data-driven trading explores how traders can use AI to interpret charts, analyse market news and gauge sentiment. Learners also examine the data and assumptions behind AI-generated insights to judge how much confidence to place in them.

According to recent reports, "The experienced traders at VARIANSE helped shape the Academy around decisions they face daily, from managing risk when markets move quickly to testing a strategy and reviewing trades after they close. We made it free so traders can learn at their own pace and return to the lessons as their experience grows.".

VARIANSE prepares to expand the Academy over time with dedicated learning tracks on forex, stocks, CFDs, options, futures, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and cryptocurrency. The planned curriculum will also cover proprietary trading, copy trading, asset management, trading platforms, introducing brokers and affiliates, and popular trading instruments.

The courses are designed by VARIANSE's expert analysts and draw on their day-to-day market analysis and practical trading experience. The aim is to help learners understand how trading decisions are made and develop a clear process for making and reviewing their own.

VARIANSE is a globally regulated leading fintech broker that combines institutional trading technology with direct market access, enabling traders, asset managers and algorithmic trading firms access to trade the financial markets.

Founded in 2015 and headquartered in London, VARIANSE serves clients in more than 100 countries. The brand is internationally regulated, including by the UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the Financial Services Commission (FSC) Mauritius, and registered by the Financial Services Commission (FSC) St. Vincents and the Grenadines.

VARIANSE is the Official Global Trading Partner of Southampton Football Club.

Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.
  • Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules.
  • According to recent reports, the firm announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

According to recent reports, the firm announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it notes can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson stated in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”.

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the firm.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson remarked.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter remarked.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The newly introduced complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

Sources indicate that on Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

According to recent reports, on Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the concern in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

In a recent development, on Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services.

He remarked Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the organization’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

According to recent reports, the dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

It has been revealed that amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS confirmed prepares for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

According to recent reports, in an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

Recent findings suggest that the growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

In a recent development, compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

Below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.

  • It has been revealed that issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S.
  • According to recent reports, “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:00 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Elon Musk’s Space Exploration Technologies Corp. today received approval from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to operate as data centers in orbit.

It has been revealed that issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.”.

According to recent reports, “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”.

Replying to Carr on X, Musk wrote that Starmind “will be a great asset to America and the world.”.

In a recent development, under the terms of the approval, the Starmind satellites are to sit in six orbital shells, or altitude bands, between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, below the 2,000-kilometer ceiling in SpaceX’s original application. Most communications will run over optical links to other satellites, including those in the Starlink network. The license itself covers a backup Ka-band radio system for emergency telemetry, tracking and command.

Recent findings suggest that the approval does come with conditions. SpaceX’s orbital debris blueprint was found to comply with the agency’s rules only for satellites below 600 kilometers, and four of the six shells sit above that line. Before deploying anything higher, SpaceX is required to file a modification application containing a final debris plan.

A request from the firm to retire some of those higher satellites into disposal orbits around Earth or the sun, rather than having them re-enter the atmosphere within five years, was deferred for lack of information.

To keep the authorization, SpaceX has to have its first Starmind satellite in operation by Nov. 25, 2033. The schedule then calls for 100,000 satellites by 2035, 500,000 by 2038 and the full 1 million by 2040. Missing any of the deadlines would void the license.

Petitions to deny the application from Amazon.com Inc.’s Amazon Leo satellite business, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society were all rejected. In a March filing, Amazon had described the initiative as “a lofty ambition rather than a real plan.”.

It has been revealed that according to the bureau, nothing in the FCC’s rules limits how many satellites a single constellation can include. Astronomers’ concerns about the satellites’ brightness in infrared were ruled to fall outside the scope of a radio license.

According to recent reports, spaceX first applied for the system in January, shortly before it acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI Corp. Orbital data centers then featured in SpaceX’s pitch to investors ahead of its record initial public offering in June. Built around a space-optimized version of Nvidia Corp.’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, the first-generation Starmind satellite, known as AI1, could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of next year, according to Musk.

Industry observers note that the competitors Carr referred to include Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin LLC, which applied in March for Project Sunrise, a planned network of up to 51,600 data center satellites. Starcloud Inc., a startup developing AI data centers in orbit, raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation in August.

Shares of SpaceX closed up 1.3% today.

Latest Update: Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious blueprint to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.
  • Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid rapidly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

In a recent development, underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

It has been revealed that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

According to recent reports, for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

Industry observers note that “I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he stated. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

It has been revealed that after graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk manufacturer developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

According to recent reports, “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd stated. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Sources indicate that redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in newly introduced natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

According to recent reports, he wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

It has been revealed that redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he noted, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd remarked, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion firm Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

In a recent development, team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd stated he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd mentioned there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when John F.
  • Kennedy presided over the family table, the children ate first, and the cranberries served with dinner came from bogs near the family’s Cape Cod retreat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when John F. Kennedy came home to Hyannis Port for his first Thanksgiving as president, his father still had the best seat in the house.

It has been revealed that joseph P. Kennedy presided over the family table, the children ate first, and the cranberries served with dinner came from bogs near the family’s Cape Cod retreat.

Five years earlier, it was what happened after Thanksgiving dinner that the family would remember. John, then a Massachusetts senator, slipped into the study off the living room with his father.

He had a list of reasons to think twice about running for president. Joseph had an answer for every one.

By the time they emerged, the Kennedys had a campaign to strategy.

The house where that conversation took place began as a summer rental. In 1926, Joseph and his wife, Rose, brought their children to Malcolm Cottage, a waterfront home overlooking Nantucket Sound. John was just 9.

According to the John F. Kennedy Hyannis Museum, Joseph bought the property two years later for $25,000 and expanded the house to accommodate his growing family.

Sources indicate that john eventually bought a place of his own behind his parents’ home. His brother Robert and sister-in-law Ethel came to own an adjoining property.

Together, the three residences formed the 6-acre compound, an arrangement that put several generations of Kennedys within walking distance of Thanksgiving dinner at the Massive House.

It has been revealed that in "White House by the Sea," author Kate Storey describes a family with surprisingly little use for a formal seating plan. Joseph and Rose took opposite ends of the mahogany table.

Everyone else picked a spot. Family cook Ziptha Anderson remembered far less flexibility when it came to carving the bird.

“They all like the same thing—the white meat,” she said.

It has been revealed that the weather had a say in the menu, too. A chilly Thanksgiving called for clam broth, while a mild afternoon meant tomato juice to start.

In a recent development, dinner was at 1 p.m. in Storey’s account of the 1956 gathering, which still left the family time for Mass and a sail before they made their way to the table.

By Thanksgiving 1961, the guest list included 13 Kennedy adults and 15 Kennedy children. There was room for another family, too. Paul Fay, then undersecretary of the Navy, joined the celebration with his wife and their three children.

Industry observers note that one family outing took the president and several of his siblings to the skating rink in Hyannis named for their late brother, Joseph Jr. John watched while Ted and his sisters rented skates and played tag on the ice.

Sources indicate that back at the compound, Bobby and Ted also got a touch football game going. That evening, the adults sat down to Vermont turkey, candied sweet potatoes, and their choice of pies.

Ted found another way to work up an appetite in 1979. A United Press International photographer caught the senator waving from his boat as he took relatives and friends sailing off Hyannis Port before Thanksgiving dinner.

Industry observers note that ethel carried on hosting Thanksgiving at Hyannis Port long after her children had families of their own. In 2010, she enlisted her son Robert to bring home two live turkeys so her grandchildren could see the birds up close. One promptly escaped.

“For three days they chased it everywhere,” Ethel told the Cape Cod Times.

A couple of months later, the newspaper ran a story about a turkey causing trouble in nearby Centerville, where it had even taken on a moving postal truck. Ethel called the newsroom. She thought she knew where the bird had come from.
