#202323. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1135 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.
  • I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.
  • We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

Sources indicate that I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Sources indicate that most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

Recent findings suggest that we eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

Sources indicate that I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

Sources indicate that not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

Recent findings suggest that I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Industry observers note that once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:.

Sources indicate that “Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”.

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

Sources indicate that if you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a fresh closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.
  • Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn.
  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Significant Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman declared the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

Industry observers note that the offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

Recent findings suggest that all of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in upcoming hires.

According to recent reports, the worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a manufacturer right now?

Sources indicate that harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

Recent findings suggest that there is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

Industry observers note that but it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one firm.

Industry observers note that hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more vital than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

According to recent reports, AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI manufacturer today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Industry observers note that hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual firm. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

Recent findings suggest that the true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue swiftly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

According to recent reports, the bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

Sources indicate that one venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

Sources indicate that 2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a organization that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

Industry observers note that 3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

According to recent reports, there are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Sources indicate that other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Industry observers note that whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Major Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a fresh role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

Among those experiences, the most common include:.

"I Never Said That" Is the Most Common Gaslighting Phrase.

Gaslighting often shows up in the responses workers hear when they raise concerns or disagree about what happened. 64% say they have had a dismissive or reality-denying phrase directed at them at work.

Meanwhile, 35% believe its prevalence has stayed about the same, and 6% say it has become less common.

Sources indicate that "If gaslighting becomes more common in a given work environment, it can undermine trust and become a retention problem," notes Haller. "Employees may ultimately feel that moving on is better than staying in an environment where they no longer feel comfortable or supported.".

  • Recent findings suggest that the Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to Latest Yorkers’ doors.
  • Sources indicate that the legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.

Amazon and Latest York City are fighting again.

Recent findings suggest that the Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to Latest Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

Sources indicate that the legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

It has been revealed that companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing Newly introduced York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the manufacturer wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”.

It has been revealed that amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

Recent findings suggest that in a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel mentioned the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 Fresh Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

It has been revealed that the standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the tech giant abruptly canceled aims to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

In a recent development, amazon stuck with its prepares for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6.

Sources indicate that city leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” stated Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”.

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

According to recent reports, amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company noted it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in Latest York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mortgage applications increased 6.1% from one week earlier, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) weekly mortgage applications survey for the week ending November 20, 2026.
  • On an unadjusted basis, the Index increased 3% compared with the previous week.
  • The refinance index increased 1% from the previous week and was 51% lower than the same week one year ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage applications increased 6.1% from one week earlier, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) weekly mortgage applications survey for the week ending November 20, 2026.

On an unadjusted basis, the Index increased 3% compared with the previous week.

The refinance index increased 1% from the previous week and was 51% lower than the same week one year ago. The seasonally adjusted purchase index increased 10% from one week earlier. The unadjusted purchase index increased 5% compared with the previous week and was 16% lower than the same week one year ago.

Sources indicate that “Mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.38%, its highest level in five weeks. While mortgage rates increased slightly on a weekly average basis, rates declined over the course of the week, which likely spurred purchase application activity,” remarked Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace.”.

Kan added that a larger share of borrowers gravitated to ARM loans. The ARM share of activity accounted for 11.5% of applications, the highest share in more than a year, Kan noted.

“At 6.39%, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week. Refinance activity was flat over the week with conventional applications showing a small increase while VA refinances dropped more than 11%,” he noted.

According to recent reports, the refinance share of mortgage activity decreased to 40.1% of total applications from 41.1% the previous week. The adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) share of activity increased to 11.5% of total applications.

By product, the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) share of total applications decreased to 15.9% from 16.1% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) share decreased to 12.4% from 12.8% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5% from the week prior.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances ($832,750 or less) increased to 7.38% from 7.35%. Meanwhile, the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with jumbo loan balances decreased to 7.29% from 7.31%.

Recent findings suggest that the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages backed by the FHA decreased to 7.05% from 7.06% while rates for 15-year fixed-rate mortgages increased to 6.79% from 6.64%. The average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs slightly increased to 6.39% from 6.38%.

Xactus’s Mortgage Intent Index — which analyzes aggregated, anonymized credit-pull activity across the Xactus Intelligent Verification Platform — increased week-over-week to a reading of 97.8.

It has been revealed that “Mortgage intent edged up approximately 2.2% week over week,” said Thomas Lloyd, chief strategy officer at Xactus. “The uptick follows last week’s Veterans Day-suppressed reading, suggesting underlying borrower demand remains present even in a challenging rate environment.”.

Lloyd continued, “Early readings from the Daily Xactus Mortgage Intent Index offer some cautious optimism heading into Thanksgiving week — Monday’s reading of 65.9 reflects expected seasonal softness, but the year-over-year gap of approximately 16.5% is a notable improvement from the roughly 25% deficit seen in recent weeks.”.

A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it.
  • Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.
  • when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

According to recent reports, sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A major part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” noted Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively newly introduced sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

According to recent reports, what you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he mentioned.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

According to recent reports, often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

Sources indicate that but that can be a long road. Sangaré noted it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

In a recent development, and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré mentioned; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

A co-living community in West Oakland, CA, has hit the market for the first time.

In a recent development, the Union is a three-house, 14-bedroom compound and is listed at $2,999,995. That’s the asking price for all three homes. If purchased separately by friends, multigenerational families, or any other buyers who want to live side by side, the starting price is $899,000 for the smallest of the three homes, which has five bedrooms and four bathrooms.

Each home is separately deeded as a condo within the greater compound.

Sources indicate that this lot has been zoned RM-3, or Mixed Housing Type Residential–3, which allows for multiple single-family homes on a single lot. This setup is permissible due to changes in California law allowing for higher-density housing in residential areas.

This project started in 2019 when a startup called Open Door bought the 7,535-square-foot empty lot and tasked Matt Baran of Baran Studio Architecture with creating a co-living space.

They asked: “What if we design something that can be beautiful design and work with the upcoming state laws that allow for increased density in neighborhoods and works well for community living?” states listing agent Max Nelson, who specializes in co-living sales through the platform Live Near Friends.

The end result was a rent-by-the-room community where residents enjoyed shared amenities, including a backyard fire pit, co-working space, and rooftop deck with views of downtown Oakland.

The design process balanced group-friendly amenities with the look and feel of the neighborhood, which is filled with mostly Victorian homes.

Nelson claims that the architects asked, “How do we create a modern house without making it look like it doesn't fit?”.

According to recent reports, the design included bay windows that jut from the homes, mirroring the style of a classic Victorian. Having three separate homes rather than one huge building also matched the aesthetic of the area, as did the incorporation of tall, narrow windows.

Much of the rest of the design leans more modern, especially the efficient energy systems. The homes rely on shared solar panels, greatly reducing energy bills. Everything is electric—there is no reliance on gas. Each room has its own fan coils to create customized comfort.

“It’s a super efficient, well-done system,” notes Nelson.

Because The Union was designed for co-living, some of the best features are the shared spaces and the flow among the three homes.

Sources indicate that the property fronting the street, 1514, has the smaller price tag at $899,000 and offers 1,919 square feet of living space, including five bedrooms and four bathrooms. A skybridge connects it with the back two condos, positioned side by side like a duplex and sharing a common wall.

It has been revealed that the larger of the back condos, 1510, is listed at $1,049,500 and sits slightly larger at 2,033 square feet, again with five bedrooms and four bathrooms. Connected is 1512, also offered at $1,049,500 with 2,015 square feet, including four bedrooms and four bathrooms.

Above these two condos is the roof area, which houses the solar panels as well as the communal deck with AstroTurf and several seating areas.

Industry observers note that it all adds up to a highly functional, thoughtfully designed compound that meets the needs of communal living. It offers both shared spaces as well as smaller decks, outdoor seating nooks, and private spaces for solo or one-on-one time with another—because shared living works best when people have the freedom to come together or enjoy time apart.

In a recent development, mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the organization’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas noted.

#202313. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (835 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, want to price more precisely?
  • Industry observers note that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

Industry observers note that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Recent findings suggest that expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer remarked yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Sources indicate that imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Sources indicate that suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

Industry observers note that it also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

Sources indicate that when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

Industry observers note that this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Industry observers note that listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

Industry observers note that so, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

In a recent development, sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

Recent findings suggest that we’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly briefed Congressional staffers about Alice Huang, the cloud executive at the center of the Jensen Huang controversy.

The classified discussion took place on Tuesday, sources told the Latest York Times and the Wall Street Journal today. It was attended by staff members of the House and Senate intelligence committees. The briefing is said to have included representatives of the FBI, CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

Sources indicate that alice Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud provider that has reportedly bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia Corp. chips. The organization is under investigation for allegedly breaching U.S. export controls. Those controls prohibit companies from selling cutting-edge artificial intelligence chips to customers in China.

The paper stated that she had been “found to be passing intelligence” to China. A few days later, other outlets reported that U.S. officials had not yet concluded that Alice Huang is a spy. The U.S. Justice Department reaffirmed that’s the case shortly thereafter.

Those agencies’ representatives reportedly “did not dispute” that she had gathered information for China. However, they stated that there’s no evidence China’s MSS spy agency directed her to initiate the affair.

Recent findings suggest that some U.S. officials reportedly believe Alice Huang can still be considered a spy. Others are noted to see her ties to the country’s intelligence service as ”more circumstantial.” According to the Journal, officials don’t believe that Alice Huang passed any “intelligence of significance” to China.

In a recent development, the briefers reportedly told Congressional staffers that Kang Wei, a businessman believed to be Huang’s husband, is a “more significant” figure. They stated that Kang is a Chinese intelligence asset who was “often” in touch with the country’s spy agency.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 12, the Journal reported that Kang had known Jensen Huang for over a decade. The publication later revealed that he had built a data center network in China.

The briefing reportedly did not cover the most sensitive information the U.S. intelligence community has gathered about Alice Huang. Additionally, it didn’t include a classified memo about her relationship with Jensen Huang that was drafted under the supervision of U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio. Congressional staffers requested a copy of the memo.

Jensen Huang is set to appear before three House committees on Dec. 1. Prior to the spy controversy, he was reportedly scheduled to make a product announcement that day. The closed-door briefing will be followed by a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Darryl Davis Seminars Inc.’s multi-million dollar federal trademark infringement lawsuit against Epique Realty, which accuses the virtual brokerage of unlawfully using the POWER AGENT® brand in its nationwide operations, is headed to court next week.

During the first week of December, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Latest York will hold a hearing on a motion for a preliminary injunction filed by Darryl Davis and his firm that would bar Epique Realty, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, from using the POWER AGENT trademark.

Originally filed in late June, the lawsuit alleges that Houston-based Epique Realty adopted the POWER AGENT name and “built an entire brand architecture around it” despite being put on notice and asked to stop, according to the announcement. In addition to Epique Realty, the lawsuit also lists Joshua Miller, Janice Delcid, Christopher Miller, XYZ Corps 1-10 and John and Jane Does 1-10 as defendants.

Darryl Davis Seminars indicates it has used the POWER AGENT mark continuously since 1993 through The POWER Program, which it describes as the real estate industry’s oldest and longest-running agent training and coaching platform.

Recent findings suggest that “POWER AGENT® has been our name since 1993, and both it and THE POWER PROGRAM® are registered trademarks,” Davis told HousingWire. “The law expects a trademark owner to protect its marks. We have for decades, and we will keep doing so. Because the matter is pending, I will let our court filings speak to the rest.”.

In October, Epique filed a counterclaim asking for a ruling from the court that Davis’s trademark registrations of Power Agent programs do not give his firm exclusive rights to the word “power” and that this does not give Davis or his manufacturer the rights to a family of “Power” trademarks. Epique is also asking the court to force Davis and his firm to prove likely confusing for each expression of “Power” Epique was accused of. Epique is also seeking rulings from the court that its current uses of PowerFlex and PowerCon, do not infringe on Davis’s trademarks and that it is not liable “merely because an independently controlled agent or third party used POWER-formative wording.”.

Recent findings suggest that epique emphasized in the filing that its agents are independent contractors and that the firm does not hold passwords for agents’ personal social media accounts in order to edit or delete content, nor does it review agents’ social media posts or websites before they are published. This contradicts Davis’s complaint, which alleges that the brokerage’s independent contractor agreement requires agents to submit marketing or advertising posts for approval prior to publication. Additionally, the company mentioned that under state law in Texas, where Epique is headquartered, the firm is only responsible for ensuring that advertising content produced by agents complies with state rules.

In a filing earlier this month, Davis largely denied Epique’s counterclaims, namely that he is trying to trademark the word “Power” by itself and he and his firm rejected Epique’s request that the court declares that Darryl Davis Seminars does not own the word “power” exclusively and that it does not have an across-the-board monopoly over trademarks containing the word. Throughout the filing, Davis maintained that Epique infringed on his firm’s trademarks and he asked the court to reject Epique’s counter claims.

Sources indicate that this news was first reported by Inman. Epique Realty did not immediately returned HousingWire’s request for comment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am.

Orchard Robotics, an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, mentioned in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

“Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu said in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”.

In a recent development, the startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

According to recent reports, orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round revealed in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

According to recent reports, the Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

FutureMain Sets Its Sights on Nasdaq, Bringing Decades of Industrial Expertise Into the AI Era

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The South Korean industrial AI company combines 38 years of engineering expertise with explainable artificial intelligence, targeting the next generation of intelligent manufacturing.
  • Sources indicate that SUWON, South Korea, Nov.
  • On September 11, 2026, FutureMain confirmed that it had entered into a definitive business combination agreement with ChampionsGate Acquisition Corp., a Nasdaq-listed special purpose acquisition manufacturer (SPAC).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The South Korean industrial AI company combines 38 years of engineering expertise with explainable artificial intelligence, targeting the next generation of intelligent manufacturing.

Sources indicate that SUWON, South Korea, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- FutureMain, a South Korean industrial artificial intelligence company specializing in machinery diagnostics and predictive and prescriptive maintenance, is pursuing a Nasdaq listing as part of its strategy to expand into global manufacturing markets.

On September 11, 2026, FutureMain confirmed that it had entered into a definitive business combination agreement with ChampionsGate Acquisition Corp., a Nasdaq-listed special purpose acquisition manufacturer (SPAC).

In a recent development, upon completion of the proposed transaction, the combined organization is expected to be listed on Nasdaq. The parties anticipate closing the transaction in 2027, subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals and other customary closing conditions.

It has been revealed that for FutureMain, the proposed listing represents more than an opportunity to raise its international profile. It is a strategic step toward building the scale, operational capacity and global service infrastructure required to serve major industrial customers.

According to recent reports, deploying new technologies across large manufacturing facilities and mission-critical production systems requires more than technical performance. Global manufacturers also demand long-term business continuity, dependable delivery capabilities and confidence in their technology partners.

Recent findings suggest that by pursuing access to the U.S. capital markets, FutureMain aims to strengthen its international business foundation and accelerate the adoption of its industrial AI technologies.

The ambition is substantial for a tech giant that began with just three people and had approximately 24 employees in early 2026.

Yet the manufacturer's vision is rooted in a problem that manufacturers around the world have faced for generations: understanding why machines fail â and preventing those failures before they disrupt operations.

Before Machines Fail, They Send Signals.

When a major manufacturing facility unexpectedly shuts down, the consequences can extend far beyond the factory floor.

Automotive production lines, pharmaceutical plants, power generation facilities and shipyards all depend on complex machinery operating reliably, often around the clock.

And before many mechanical failures occur, equipment begins to exhibit subtle changes.

Sources indicate that A vibration too faint for the human ear to detect. A temperature variation that is difficult to observe directly. An unusual pattern hidden within operational data.

For decades, experienced maintenance engineers have relied on specialized knowledge and practical experience to interpret these signals.

But what if artificial intelligence could learn to apply the diagnostic expertise accumulated by engineers over generations?

What if industrial equipment could be monitored not simply to detect abnormal conditions, but to identify emerging risks, explain their underlying causes and recommend appropriate maintenance actions?

That is the future FutureMain is working to create.

Turning 38 Years of Engineering Knowledge Into Industrial AI.

The global artificial intelligence industry is advancing rapidly, with companies competing to develop increasingly capable models and applications.

Yet applying AI effectively in real industrial environments remains a fundamentally different challenge.

A factory cannot be fully understood through information learned from the internet alone.

Similar vibration patterns may indicate entirely different mechanical problems depending on equipment design, operating conditions and the physical mechanisms involved.

For plant operators, an alarm indicating that something is abnormal is rarely sufficient to justify stopping a critical production line.

What matters is understanding not only what is wrong, but why it is happening and what should be done next.

FutureMain developed its flagship ExRBM platform to address precisely this challenge.

Founded in 2014, the company has incorporated 38 years of accumulated machinery diagnostic engineering expertise from power plants, industrial facilities and manufacturing environments into its AI-based technologies.

ExRBM combines expert knowledge of mechanical failure mechanisms with machine learning, deep learning and actual equipment data.

Rather than relying solely on statistical anomaly detection, the platform is designed to identify specific failure mechanisms, explain the evidence behind its assessments and recommend appropriate responses.

According to organization disclosures, ExRBM can automatically identify more than 85 machinery failure mechanisms, including bearing damage and shaft misalignment.

In 100 tests conducted by the Korea Testing Laboratory (KTL), the technology recorded a reported automatic diagnostic accuracy of 98.3% under the specified test conditions.

FutureMain also reports 25 patents and international recognition, including a gold medal at the International Exhibition of Inventions Geneva.

The manufacturer believes its most key advantage, however, cannot be measured by the speed at which an algorithm is developed.

It lies in the depth of engineering knowledge embedded within that algorithm.

Decades of experience analyzing normal equipment behavior, abnormal operating conditions and mechanical failures have produced a specialized body of knowledge that is difficult to replicate through software development alone.

By transforming this expertise into AI-driven diagnostic capabilities, FutureMain aims to make advanced industrial knowledge more accessible, scalable and actionable.

Proven Across Industries, From Battery Manufacturing to Shipbuilding.

Industrial AI must ultimately demonstrate its value where it matters most: in operating manufacturing facilities.

FutureMain's technologies have been deployed across more than 10 industrial sectors, including battery manufacturing, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology, power generation, energy, shipbuilding and defense.

Its customer references include LG Energy Solution, Hanwha Ocean and Handok.

According to the tech giant's 2026 investor presentation, ExRBM recorded 25 deployments over the preceding three years, while FutureMain's total customer base exceeded 48 companies.

Several customer relationships have also progressed beyond initial deployments.

At Handok's Eumseong pharmaceutical manufacturing facility, applications have expanded from equipment predictive maintenance into the integration of production-process data and quality anomaly detection across granulation, coating and tablet-compression processes.

At Hanwha Ocean, machinery diagnostic applications have been extended to additional equipment following earlier system installations.

FutureMain's collaboration with LG Energy Solution is also moving toward broader applications across domestic and overseas manufacturing operations.

The organization is expanding into robotics as well.

In 2026, FutureMain has been carrying out a large-scale predictive maintenance implementation project involving welding robots and traversing equipment at HD Hyundai Construction Equipment's Ulsan facility.

These developments reflect the firm's transition from solving individual machinery problems toward building an industrial AI platform applicable across different equipment types, production processes and manufacturing sectors.

International expansion is another area of focus.

FutureMain reports that it has completed a proof-of-concept evaluation at a Saudi Aramco facility and is extending its business network across the Middle East, Southeast Asia and Japan.

From its origins in Suwon, South Korea, the manufacturer is positioning its industrial AI technology for a broader role in global manufacturing.

ExRBM 2.0: Moving From Monitoring to Explainable Intelligence.

In November 2026, FutureMain introduced ExRBM 2.0 at an AIoT technology presentation held at COEX in Seoul.

The next-generation platform represents an evolution from conventional equipment monitoring toward AI-assisted diagnosis and maintenance decision-making.

Traditional monitoring systems typically generate alerts when vibration, temperature or other operating parameters exceed predefined thresholds.

ExRBM 2.0 takes a more advanced approach.

By analyzing collected equipment data, the platform is designed to identify potential faults, explain their underlying causes and recommend appropriate maintenance actions.

A central feature is explainable artificial intelligence, or XAI, which allows consumers to examine the reasoning and evidence supporting an AI-generated diagnosis.

This distinction is particularly important in industrial environments.

When a critical machine is at risk of failure, engineers cannot always act on an unexplained warning.

They need to understand the nature of the suspected defect, the relevant frequency characteristics, the location or timing of abnormal signals and the maintenance actions that may be required.

By providing this context, ExRBM 2.0 aims to support more informed and confident decision-making.

FutureMain has also presented capabilities connecting machinery diagnostics with remaining useful life (RUL) estimation, maintenance work orders and automated diagnostic reporting.

RUL estimation is applicable depending on equipment characteristics and the availability and quality of relevant data.

In addition, the manufacturer has introduced the concept of an AI assistant based on a small language model (sLLM), enabling people to interact with machinery information and maintenance records through natural-language queries.

Instead of manually navigating multiple diagnostic screens, an engineer could ask:.

"What problem has been detected in this machine?".

"Which component should be inspected first?".

"How should we determine the appropriate maintenance timing?".

The objective is not to replace experienced engineers.

It is to preserve, transfer and extend their specialized knowledge, allowing more industrial professionals to benefit from advanced diagnostic expertise.

Beyond Predictive Maintenance: AI That Understands the Entire Factory.

FutureMain's long-term strategy extends well beyond machinery diagnostics.

The company is pursuing a manufacturing-focused vertical AI platform that connects equipment health, production processes, quality management and robotics.

Modern manufacturing facilities generate enormous volumes of data, including machinery vibration, electrical current, temperature, process pressure, equipment load and quality inspection results.

When these data sources are analyzed independently, manufacturers may identify isolated problems without understanding their broader operational relationships.

FutureMain sees an opportunity to connect them.

By integrating equipment-condition data with production and quality information, industrial AI could move beyond detecting individual machinery faults to understanding more complex interactions across manufacturing operations.

The firm's longer-term vision includes industrial AI agents capable of interpreting factory-wide conditions, analyzing operational risks and recommending appropriate responses.

Robotics represents another potential growth area.

As industrial robots become more widely deployed, technologies capable of diagnosing their mechanical condition and identifying emerging failure patterns may become increasingly important.

FutureMain is conducting research into technologies that learn normal and abnormal robotic operating patterns, on-device AI and Physical AI applications tailored to industrial environments.

Some of these initiatives remain in research and development.

Nevertheless, the firm's strategic direction is clear: to build on its established machinery diagnostic expertise and expand toward AI systems that understand manufacturing processes, product quality and the increasingly interconnected relationship between humans and robots.

A Vision Built on Real-World Expertise.

The ultimate purpose of industrial AI is not defined solely by the complexity of its algorithms or the number of patents behind it.

Its value can be found in more fundamental outcomes.

Helping prevent unexpected machinery shutdowns.

Supporting safer working environments.

Enabling more informed decisions where experienced specialists are in short supply.

And helping manufacturers produce the goods that society depends on with greater reliability.

While much of the world's attention is focused on the latest advances in generative AI, FutureMain believes the physical signals produced by industrial machinery remain an essential source of intelligence.

Behind those signals are decades of engineering knowledge and practical experience.

Shine Lee, FutureMain's Chief Operating Officer and a founding member who joined the company when it consisted of just three people, believes that this foundation will become increasingly key as the AI market matures.

It has been revealed that "Today, countless AI-powered products and services are being created, only to disappear as rapidly as they emerge," Lee noted. "AI services without deep technological foundations can easily be replaced by similar offerings. In an increasingly crowded AI market, what truly matters is building AI on technologies and expertise that cannot be easily replicated.".

Lee emphasized the importance of connecting artificial intelligence with the physical realities of manufacturing.

"Understanding real industrial equipment requires going directly into factories, examining machinery, installing sensors and collecting reliable physical data," she said. "The ability to acquire that data and transform it into meaningful intelligence for AI-driven decision-making is what FutureMain does best. It is also the foundation of our long-term competitive advantage.".

Looking ahead, Lee described a vision that extends beyond traditional engineering AI.

"Our ambition is to evolve into a Hyperconnected Autonomous AI manufacturer â one where data from across the factory is seamlessly interconnected, enabling manufacturing operations to pursue optimal efficiency and continuous self-improvement.".

This vision reflects FutureMain's belief that the next generation of industrial AI will be defined not simply by more powerful models, but by deeper integration with the physical world.

Building the Next Generation of Industrial Intelligence.

FutureMain's journey, supported by 38 years of accumulated engineering expertise and a team of approximately 24 employees in early 2026, is moving beyond South Korea toward new opportunities in global manufacturing.

The proposed Nasdaq listing could represent an vital milestone in that journey.

Yet the tech giant's larger ambition is not defined by a stock market valuation.

It is rooted in the belief that AI capable of understanding real industrial environments can contribute to safer workplaces, more productive factories and a more resilient manufacturing ecosystem.

Around the world, millions of machines continue to operate inside factories, power plants, shipyards and industrial facilities.

Each generates signals that reveal something about its condition.

FutureMain is working to transform those signals into actionable intelligence â connecting decades of engineering expertise with the capabilities of modern AI.

The future of manufacturing may depend not only on making machines more intelligent, but on giving artificial intelligence a deeper understanding of the physical world.

And for FutureMain, that future is already taking shape on the factory floor.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

In a recent development, the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

In a recent development, “Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

Industry observers note that “The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

It has been revealed that the terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

Industry observers note that “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an crucial step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Industry observers note that inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

In a recent development, the solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

Recent findings suggest that “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel noted. “I think it’s notable to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker noted workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

It has been revealed that tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.
