📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.

It has been revealed that I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape.

While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.

Industry observers note that my inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.

If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.

In a recent development, as a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering.

Industry observers note that modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era, when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved.

In her book “Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event.

In a recent development, within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity.

Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a latest recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.

What’s your apocalypse skill? Finding a future‑proof hobby can bring fulfilment today.

Five ways to enjoy fashion as a hobby without indulging in overconsumption.

The ick: The psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you.

Today, Thanksgiving is typically viewed as a family holiday.

For some, this may be the gathering that provides the warm, fuzzy holiday feeling many search for. But for others, family holidays are stressful.

A 2023 survey of 2,061 adults found that 9 in 10 people reported experiencing stress around money, lost loved ones, familial conflict or other expectations during the holidays.

Industry observers note that as Friendsgiving isn’t an established holiday, participation is difficult to capture. But of 1,000 people surveyed in 2024, 20% said they planned to celebrate Friendsgiving.

A Friendsgiving is the opposite of established kin-keeping traditions. It gives the opportunity to gather with found family, and while the reason for gathering is established, the form is malleable.

Recent findings suggest that many people choose a potluck-style as a way of sharing the burden for what can be a labor-intensive meal. Others choose to do away entirely with what is considered the “traditional” meal and showcase foods from their own culture or a cuisine they enjoy.

In a recent development, as a parody of a holiday, Friendsgiving gives participants permission to make the holiday their own and be as playful as they wish. So, if I burn my miso butter corn casserole, no one will be disappointed, because they’ve never tasted it before anyway.

While playing with form and bucking traditional structure can be rewarding, there are some things you may want to keep in mind to have a successful Friendsgiving.

According to recent reports, in her book “The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why it Matters,” author Priya Parker advises anyone planning a gathering to be specific about purpose. This will help decide the form of the event and whom to invite.

Recent findings suggest that is this a casual gathering with friends? Is fellowship or food more crucial? Are you hoping to try a recipe your family would never approve? Be specific about your own expectations before you start planning.

The Emily Post Institute, which promotes etiquette and offers resources for a variety of social situations, recommends being flexible with the menu. This is especially important for a potluck-style gathering. As a host, you may want to assign dishes to guests to ensure a balanced meal without eight desserts. If you have the gumption, however, you can throw caution to the wind and see what happens.

It is also notable to keep dietary restrictions in mind to make sure everyone feels included and has something to eat.

Industry observers note that make a blueprint for heating or reheating. The oven is prime real estate during Thanksgiving. You may want to tell guests to bring their dish already cooked to avoid playing oven Tetris.

Finally, tell guests to bring Tupperware. There will be leftovers, and I have found that nothing is better than creating a second plate to take home and heat up the next day.

Alice P. Julier, a professor of food studies at Chatham University, assisted with the writing of this article.

Kirsten Chervenak, Research Associate for the Center for Regional Agriculture, Food, and Transformation, Chatham University.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that BYD just got some good news in its Defender-copycat court battle with JLR. After JLR had BYD’s Netherlands offices raided and documents seized, a Dutch court has now handed BYD an early win, ordering JLR to destroy the documents or face a penalty.

After BYD opened orders for the Ti 7 in Europe and the UK in late July, many (including us at Electrek) compared it to the iconic Land Rover Defender, with its boxy, rugged (yet still elegant) SUV design.

BYD even described it as having “an unapologetically boxy profile” that delivers “the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look.”.

In August, authorities on behalf of the British luxury automaker raided BYD’s offices in the Netherlands without prior warning and seized digital records.

On November 11, a Dutch court in The Hague ruled against JLR and ordered the organization to destroy the seized documents, which included launch intends and other technical data, so they wouldn’t fall into anyone else’s hands.

JLR must destroy the documents within 24 hours of the ruling or face a fine of €50,000 ($55,000) for every hour it is delayed, with a maximum penalty of up to €500,000 ($553,000).

Within 24 hours of destroying it, JLR must also provide BYD with third-party confirmation that it has been destroyed. The court also rejected the British automaker’s request to pay a €500,000 ($553,000) fine.

According to Autoweek Netherlands, the ruling is based on the fact that JLR doesn’t need the documents, noting that the Ti 7 has not yet been sold in the European Union.

BYD won the ruling, and JLR is prohibited from taking any further legal action under the initial seizure order, but JLR has already begun summary proceedings over the infringement in Rotterdam and The Hague.

JLR claims that the Ti 7 SUV is a “slavish imitation” and infringes on the intellectual property of the Land Rover Defender and that BYD stripped down the Defender to reverse-engineer some of its technology.

Before the raid, BYD claims it fully cooperated with JLR’s requests. BYD’s lawyers called the British automakers’ raid a “fishing expedition” and claimed that “too many files were seized.”.

The Ti 7 is on sale starting at £47,995 ($64,000) in the UK, on the road. That’s over £20,000 ($26,500) less than the plug-in Defender 110, which starts at £71,840 ($95,500) in the UK.

It has a seven-seat arrangement, which BYD mentioned was specifically designed for the European and UK markets.

As the first vehicle in the UK based on its DM-p (Dual Mode performance) powertrain, BYD stated the Ti 7 “vastly exceeds the closest competition,” seemingly another jab at the Defender.

"JLR believes BYD stripped down the Defender to reverse engineer some of its technology".

Reverse engineering isn't illegal. Patent infringement is illegal.

Competition strip down each other's product all the time. As long as they don't use the "exact" same technology, it isn't a copy right matter.

The setup uses three electric motors and a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine, delivering a combined 402 hp (408 PS), enabling it to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph in 4.8 seconds.

Sources indicate that the engine primarily powers a 35.6 kWh BYD Blade Battery, which provides a pure-electric WLTP driving range of up to 74 miles. In the city, it has an electric range of up to 102 miles.

Available exclusively in the UK in the flagship Excellence AWD trim, BYD claims that the Ti 7 offers “a level of equipment that exceeds anything that its rivals can offer at this price point.”.

We should learn more about the BYD and JLR legal battle soon. Check back for updates, as this story is still ongoing.

From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.
  • Since Grant Canary released his company a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary released his company a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

The company recently shifted again, adding a upcoming line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary remarked, which benefits everyone.

Industry observers note that just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

According to recent reports, high school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the issues.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

When I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there rapidly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

It has been revealed that I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

It has been revealed that that ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

My personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally notable: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [Upcoming York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do significant things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

In a recent development, in the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

According to recent reports, AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

My hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as major an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Hoskinson, founder of Cardano (ADA), has tried to clear the air regarding the utility of the cryptocurrency. This comes as ADA has fallen more than 95% from its all-time high.

Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson responded to frustrated Cardano community members who are disappointed by the blockchain’s pace of development and inability to rebound from the current slump.

On Nov. 21, Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson took to X to counter criticism about the current state of Cardano.

The exchange was triggered by a joke made by an X user stating that Grand Theft Auto 6 came out before a working Cardano blockchain.

Hoskinson replied to the comment, saying: “Cardano works.”.

Later, Hoskinson addressed the poor price performance of the cryptocurrency and explained that price doesn’t always reflect the capabilities of blockchain networks.

Recent findings suggest that “Yeah. Price doesn't equal utility. Is Solana 75 percent less capable than it's all time high? It's an infinitely better product today for many more people. And so it is for Cardano,” he remarked.

What this means is that even if the value of a blockchain network's native cryptocurrency is dropping, the technology can still advance.

An X user, however, contested his comparison with Solana, stating that Cardano hasn’t been able to retake its previous all-time high even after years of development.

This drew an increasingly irritated response from Hoskinson.

Sources indicate that “So every single thing a f****** scam? Everything they do failed? I’m so tired of you people,” said the Cardano founder.

This recent statement by Hoskinson comes as Cardano (ADA) remains one of the worst-performing major cryptocurrencies in the current market downturn.

As per CoinGlass data, ADA is presently trading at around $0.14. The cryptocurrency is down by about 57% since the beginning of 2026.

It has lost a whopping 95.4% of its value from its all-time high of $3.09, set in September 2021.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 21, ADA briefly dipped toward $0.13. This came as another sell-off hit the broader crypto market.

Cardano has been in a steady decline, leading to criticism regarding its adoption, activity in its ecosystem and ability to compete with the likes of Ethereum and Solana.

Nonetheless, Charles Hoskinson has maintained that short-term market performance should not be conflated with the progress of blockchain technology over the long run.

Earlier this month, the Cardano founder tried to reassure frustrated ADA holders and tell them that things would eventually get better.

“It's all going to be ok. Everyone will be happy next year after all this madness, hate and idiocy,” said Hoskinson in a previous X post.
